items.title: Trump threatens to double tariffs on Mexico if it does not halt migrants
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump on Thursday threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if it does not stop more than a thousand migrants walking north toward the United States after last week's US election, warning that they would not be allowed to enter.

"Here we go again!" Trump wrote on social media. "They will not be accepted! MEXICO MUST STOP THEM, NOW, and if they do not do so, the Tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED. MEXICO, THE GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, THE VERY LIBERAL NEW GOVERNOR OF TEXAS, OUR GREAT BORDER PATROL, & ICE, HAVE BEEN SO INFORMED. There will be no leniency!"

The group of migrants, an estimated 1,500 people mostly from Central America, set off on Tuesday from the southern city of Tapachula near the Guatemala border, hoping Democrats' victory in the US midterm election could open pathways for them to live and work in the United States.

There was no immediate response from Mexican government officials.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum was due to hold a news conference Thursday morning.

Trump's threat about the caravan comes as the US and Mexico negotiate a trade deal, after he chose in July to not extend the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade pact.

The Trump administration's tough immigration policies mostly stopped the flow of migrants to the US southern border, leaving many Mexican migrant shelters empty.

Trump was re-elected in 2024 in part over US voters' concern about the border. Since then, the president has highlighted some migrant caravans but also said in recent months the issue has become less politically potent for him and his Republican party.

"I am sure the new governor is going to want to have security at the Texas border," Trump told reporters after the November 3 midterm election, referencing the newly elected Texas governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Trump's migrant warning also comes as Trump acknowledged political backlash from his administration's deportation program through US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

On Sunday, Trump told CBS' '60 Minutes' the deportation force had been "too tough" and that he was open to making an immigration deal with Democrats after they take control of the US Congress in January.

Reporting by Susan Heavey and Bo Erickson in Washington; additional reporting by Paolo Laudani in Gdansk; editing by Doina Chiacu

items.title: Can a new US Congress mean an end to the Iran war?
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 12 - The American public wants the unpopular eight-month-long war on Iran to end, and showed it by handing President Donald Trump's Republicans a resounding defeat in last week's congressional elections.

Trump acknowledged that unhappiness about the conflict contributed to his party's losses, but defends the war, both insisting that he has won it and saying it will continue.

Congress cannot unilaterally end the war, but can pressure the president to do so.

Here are some ways lawmakers in the new Congress — which is scheduled to be sworn in on January 3 — can push to end the fighting.

MONEY TALKS, AS DO SHUTDOWNS

Under the US Constitution, Congress decides how federal funds should be spent. Trump has asked the House of Representatives and Senate to approve a huge increase in the defense budget — from about $950 billion to $1.5 trillion, plus an additional $67 billion for the war.

Democrats say they will not approve such a massive budget next year. But they also have proposed cutting off funding for the war even before the new Congress is seated, suggesting that anti-war Republicans or fiscal hawks concerned about the deficit might back them.

The current government funding bill expires on December 11, meaning Congress must pass a full-year budget or a short-term spending plan to avoid a shutdown right before Christmas, interfering with travel and putting thousands out of work.

House Republican leaders say the party will hold firm behind Trump.

"A Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto, so if that's their (the Democrats') demand, well, we'll just wait until next year," Representative Tom Cole of Oklahoma, who chairs the House Appropriations Committee, told reporters this week.

But once the Democrats control Congress, they can include clauses in budget bills forbidding the use of any funds for hostilities against Iran. Trump could issue vetoes, but would again risk a government shutdown, and potentially no pay for the troops themselves, in order to prolong the war.

Congress can also refuse to authorize any funding for the war in the annual National Defense Authorization Act, or NDAA, which sets policy for the Pentagon. Since the NDAA has passed every year since 1961, its failure would be an embarrassment for both parties.

LEGISLATION

Trump did not secure approval from Congress before he launched the war alongside Israel on February 28, and Democrats, along with a few Republicans, have voted repeatedly to end the fighting unless he seeks congressional authorization.

One of these war powers resolutions passed both the House and Senate, but Trump's administration ignored it, and legal experts said there is no consensus on whether it was binding.

Democrats have vowed to keep pushing, and expect votes on more war powers resolutions, with more legislation promised once they control the House and Senate.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll this month showed 71% of Americans — including 93% of Democrats and 51% of Republicans — want Congress to pass legislation ending the conflict.

Trump is expected to veto any measure to stop the fighting. It takes two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override a veto, meaning Democrats would need Republican support to overcome Trump's objections.

However, backers say it is worth trying, to send a message to Trump, and the American public, that many members of Congress want the fighting to stop.

They also say that sentiments might change, even among Republicans, if the war drags on.

OVERSIGHT

An effort led by Republican Representative Thomas Massie and backed mainly by Democrats to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on charges including waging the Iran war without congressional approval failed this week. But Democrats may try again next year, viewing Hegseth as the individual most responsible for the war, after Trump.

Once they are in charge of congressional committees, Democrats can hold hearings and launch investigations into the Trump administration's strategy, spending and conduct of the war. And they will have the power to issue subpoenas to compel testimony.

Individual members of Congress and Democrats on congressional committees have already been sending letters to the State and Defense departments asking for the preservation of documents associated with decision-making on the war.

If the administration refuses to cooperate with such inquiries, Congress can apply pressure, such as by withholding funding for officials' travel budgets or, in the case of the Senate, by declining to confirm Trump's nominees.

items.title: Vance, Rubio, Ossoff and Buttigieg lead 2028 White House hopefuls, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Four potential contenders in the 2028 race for the White House have caught American voters' attention with their early jockeying: Republicans JD Vance and Marco Rubio and Democrats Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.

None of the four has yet formally launched a campaign and the parties' 2028 nominating contests are more than a year away, leaving plenty of time for new contenders to emerge and for voters' views to change.

Some 45% of Republican voters polled said they believed Secretary of State Rubio would be an "excellent" presidential candidate, with 43% saying the same of Vice President Vance. Former Transportation Secretary Buttigieg and US Senator Ossoff, of Georgia, each got that rating from 29% of Democratic voters.

The poll, which surveyed 1,705 US adults nationwide including roughly 500 registered voters from each party and was completed on Monday, had a margin of error of 5 percentage points for Republican and Democratic voters.

President Donald Trump, struggling with an approval rating near the lowest of his career, looms large over the conversation for both parties. Republicans are divided on whether they want a candidate who breaks with Trump or follows in his footsteps, while Democrats, who are flying high after routing Republicans in the November 3 congressional elections, are divided on how aggressively to go after the president, such as through impeachment.

Trump has quizzed allies on whom they prefer Vance or Rubio and in a Sunday interview with CBS's "60 Minutes" said he would "not necessarily" make an endorsement in the Republican primary.

'MANAGED TO DO HIS JOB'

Barbara Rezner, an attorney in Florida who voted for Trump in the last three presidential elections, said she prefers Rubio over Vance, whom she considers too far to the right and too close to the president.

"Rubio has managed to do his job. He's stayed off most people's radar because he hasn't done anything too far left, too far right, too crazy," Rezner said.

The modest but growing dissatisfaction with Trump among Republicans is centered on the president's decision to launch a war on Iran that has driven fuel prices higher. Rubio has been notably absent from many of the so-far fruitless peace talks with Iran despite being the nation's top diplomat. Vance has shown signs of wanting to distance himself as well, saying publicly that the Republican drubbing in the midterm elections owed to the war with Iran.

A dozen-odd other Republicans are also in the national conversation over 2028 contenders, with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis among the best regarded, with 32% of Republicans rating him as an excellent option. Others - like Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr., and Texas US Senator Ted Cruz - have their fans, but also many detractors.

OSSOFF AND BUTTIGIEG

Among Democrats, Ossoff is at the top of many voters' lists, with 29% of the party's registered voters rating him as excellent. Ossoff has grabbed headlines in recent months by calling Trump corrupt and unfit for office in unusually direct language, and last week he won his re-election race by 18 percentage points in Georgia, a state Trump carried by 2 points in 2024.

Buttigieg also gets the excellent rating from 29% of Democrats. Buttigieg also ran for president in 2020 and is better known nationally than Ossoff.

About one in five Democrats say they have never heard of Buttigieg, compared to roughly one in three who say the same about Ossoff. Very few Republicans are unfamiliar with Vance, but about one in six said they do not know who Rubio is. For candidates in either party, starting the election cycle with more name recognition can save money that would be spent getting the candidate's name out, but examples abound of little-known candidates catching fire during the campaign, as happened with former President Bill Clinton.

Buttigieg and Ossoff are considered moderates among Democrats, and that appeals to Democratic voters like Ed Blair, a retired pig farmer in southern Illinois, who gives Buttigieg a better rating in part because Ossoff is less familiar.

"I do favor the more moderate candidates over the more progressive ones," said Blair, who is wary of proposed major shifts like expanding federal Medicare health insurance coverage from all seniors to everyone in the country. Blair would prefer gradual shifts, such as expanding Medicare to cover all children. "In going towards some of the progressive policies, small steps need to be taken rather than large ones to give people time to adapt."

The Reuters/Ipsos poll shows other well-known moderates - like former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in the 2024 presidential election, and California Governor Gavin Newsom - each get "excellent candidate" ratings of 23%, higher than the 15% of Democrats who view progressive stalwart Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a US representative for New York, that way.

Ocasio-Cortez told CNN after the midterms that impeaching Trump should be an option on the table, while Buttigieg told the New Yorker magazine he is "not very interested" in impeachment.

Elaine Kamarck, a Democratic strategist, cautioned against reading too deeply into the public's current views this far out from the 2028 election. "It's a world away," Kamarck said. "There are lots of people in both parties who are still deciding if they are going to run. You might be able to predict who will run, but you certainly don't know anything about who is going to be ahead."

Reporting by Tim Reid and Jason Lange; Editing by Scott Malone and Alistair Bell

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US FDA shelves commissioner's voucher program for speedy drug reviews, sources say
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The US Food and Drug Administration has shelved the fast-track drug review initiative launched during the Trump administration by former Commissioner Marty Makary, according to six sources familiar with the matter and internal documents.

Launched in June 2025, the Commissioner's National Priority Voucher program aimed to slash drug review timelines to just one to two months for therapies addressing national priorities, such as urgent unmet health needs. However, critics pointed to possible preferential treatment for companies meeting demands of President Donald Trump, like offering drugs at lower prices.

Once touted as a bold fix for US pharmaceutical regulation, the program has been left adrift, offering a stark window into the internal chaos, infighting, and lack of steady leadership that have plagued the FDA, which has been without a commissioner since May.

Of the 22 drugs given a voucher, a dozen have been approved, including five since Makary left the FDA in May. For several drugs, the program sped approval by eight months or more.

However, no new drugs have gotten a voucher since Makary's departure, and a key component of the program — an executive council of political appointees that oversaw drug reviews and had a central role in speeding approvals — has gone dormant, internal documents show.

Details of the voucher program being shelved have not been previously reported.

The pilot had drawn fierce criticism from regulatory experts over the handpicking of drugs and makeup of the council, which included former acting drug center director Tracy Beth Hoeg and former biologics chief Vinay Prasad. Both left the FDA earlier this year.

A source familiar with the process said companies were told by FDA leadership that the agency is not moving forward with the program but is keeping applications open. When companies submit them, they don't advance, he said.

Rich Danker, a former assistant secretary at the Department of Health and Human Services, said the initiative is quietly being phased out, pointing to the departure of the program's top administrator. No new vouchers have been awarded, he said.

HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard said the pilot is ongoing and that the FDA is reviewing feedback from a June public hearing on it to refine the framework.

The agency did not respond to requests for comment regarding the departure of the program's lead or whether a new program coordinator had been appointed.

'WORST OF BOTH WORLDS'

Holly Fernandez Lynch, a health policy professor at the University of Pennsylvania, described the program as "the worst of both worlds," combining serious risks of political influence with potentially limited practical benefit since many drugs might have qualified for other speedy (review) pathways.

During the June public hearing on the pilot, former FDA executive Peter Lurie criticized the program for ceding review decisions to political appointees, risking consumer safety with compressed timelines, and lacking transparency, echoing other medical experts, patient groups, and industry figures.

The review of Sanofi's (SASY.PA) diabetes drug Tzield is one example of the role the council played in the approval process. Tasked with evaluating the recommendation from the primary review team, Hoeg withheld her approval of the drug. At three separate executive council meetings between October 2025 and April, she repeatedly raised safety objections.

After she and Makary left, agency staff quickly granted accelerated approval in June.

Hoeg, a sports medicine physician who opposed COVID-19 vaccines and pandemic policies, told Reuters she is concerned about children being prescribed Tzield, saying a clinical trial showed "minimal at most" benefit when weighed against the product's safety risks.

Sanofi said the FDA concluded the drug's benefits outweighed the risks and detailed its scientific rationale in a public memo.

Critics noted awards granted to companies that reached drug-pricing deals with the White House, such as Eli Lilly (LLY.N) and Novo Nordisk (NOVOb.CO). Germany's Merck KGaA (MRCG.DE) said in August it received a voucher for its fertility treatment Pergoveris as part of its drug-price agreement with the administration this year.

Lilly, Novo and Merck KGaA declined to comment.

VOUCHER DRUGS MOVE FORWARD WITHOUT COUNCIL REVIEW

Of the two latest voucher applications for new drugs cleared since Makary left — Merck's (MRK.N) cholesterol pill Lipfendra and Revolution Medicines' (RVMD.O) pancreatic cancer drug Rasonque — neither was vetted by the executive council, documents show. Rasonque was approved on a swift timeline typical for breakthrough cancer therapies using the agency's preexisting oncology review mechanisms.

Despite a high-profile Oval Office rollout with the company's CEO last year to tout new fertility initiatives, Merck KGaA's supposedly prioritized Pergoveris remains unapproved three months after the FDA accepted its final application following an eight-month rolling review.

Merck KGaA and Revolution declined to comment on the review process, while US-based Merck did not respond to a comment request.

For the nine drugs still in the program, FDA career scientists have resumed overseeing review timelines, two sources said.

Reporting by Patrick Wingrove in London and Yasmeen Abutaleb in Washington; Editing by Caroline Humer and Bill Berkrot

items.title: Florida city says it will not host St Patrick's Day parade, Pride event due to anti-diversity law
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A city in Florida said it will not host its annual St. Patrick's Day Parade or Pride event in 2027 due to a state law signed by Republican Governor Ron DeSantis that prohibits local governments from promoting or funding diversity initiatives.

The city of Delray Beach said in a statement that restrictions under the law "include certain programming and activities designed or implemented with reference to ethnicity, sexual orientation, or gender identity."

Mayor Tom Carney said on social media the city was "working feverishly with multiple entities to ensure the 2027 St. Patrick's Day parade goes on as scheduled."

St. Patrick's Day in March honors Ireland's patron saint and Irish culture and heritage. Pride festivals celebrate LGBTQ communities.

The bill was signed by DeSantis in April and takes effect on January 1.

Republican state leaders and US President Donald Trump's administration have rallied against diversity, equity and inclusion practices, casting them as discriminatory against groups like white people and men.

At the federal level, Trump has signed executive orders aimed at dismantling such initiatives and has threatened to freeze funds for educational institutions over diversity programs.

Civil rights advocates say diversity initiatives help address historic inequities for marginalized groups like the LGBT community, women and ethnic minorities.

DeSantis says the law requires grant recipients to certify that public funds will not be used to advance such initiatives and provides enforcement mechanisms, including penalties for officials who violate the law.

Last week, the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the largest US Muslim advocacy group, suspended operations in Florida after the enforcement of a separate law that gave state officials power to designate groups as "terrorist organizations."

items.title: Trump's ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in the spotlight
items.content_html:
November 12 - President Donald Trump's close ties with Nvidia (NVDA.O) CEO Jensen Huang have come under renewed scrutiny after revelations about the billionaire executive's affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Trump said on Monday he was "amazed" after the revelations concerning one of his closest allies in Silicon Valley, who also faces an FBI probe as well as a board meeting to decide his future.

Over the past two years, Huang has voiced support for the Trump administration's AI agenda and met the Republican leader many times as Nvidia sought to sell advanced chips to the Chinese market and lobbied for looser restrictions on Chinese access to Nvidia's sophisticated AI chips.

Democratic and Republican lawmakers have called to halt exports of advanced AI chips to China. Huang and the White House have argued that continuing US sales to China would keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology.

Here is a timeline on some publicly known interactions and meetings between the Nvidia CEO and Trump since the Republican leader returned to the White House in January 2025:

JANUARY 2025:

Trump met the Nvidia boss during the first month of his return to the White House, casting the interaction as a good meeting.

JULY 2025:

The Nvidia CEO met Trump at the White House before Huang's visit to China.

Later in the month, Trump gave a shout out to Huang as he spoke and signed executive orders at an AI summit.

"Jensen, will you stand up? What a job, what a job you've done," Trump remarked. "He's a great guy too."

AUGUST 2025:

Huang met Trump at the White House as the Trump administration and Nvidia engaged in talks over allowing advanced AI chip sales to China.

SEPTEMBER 2025:

Huang joined Trump during a state visit to Britain.

NOVEMBER 2025:

The Nvidia CEO attended a US-Saudi Arabia investment forum in Washington during the first visit of Saudi Arabian Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to the US capital since 2018. Huang talked about the future of AI at the event.

DECEMBER 2025:

Trump praised Huang when the Nvidia CEO visited Washington and met the Republican leader, who said the chip executive was aware of where he stood on export controls.

Huang was in the US capital that day to meet lawmakers and told them that state-by-state US regulations would slow the progress of AI development.

JANUARY 2026:

The Trump administration began allowing some exports of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China on a case-by-case basis but it did not lift the restrictions applying to organizations that Washington had put on a trade restriction list.

MARCH 2026:

In late March, the White House announced Huang as part of a 13-member council formally called the "President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology" to weigh in on AI policy and other issues.

MAY 2026:

Huang was among a delegation of tech CEOs who joined Trump during his visit to China to meet Xi as the Republican leader aimed to urge Beijing to "open up" to US business.

Trump, in a last minute addition to his May trip to China, asked Huang to join him. The Nvidia CEO was spotted boarding Air Force One during a re-fuelling stop in Alaska en route to Beijing.

SEPTEMBER 2026:

As the Trump administration and AI companies faced increasing scrutiny over risks posed by advanced AI, Trump said on September 29 that Huang was among a number of AI CEOs who signed a voluntary safety pact and backed data center expansion.

Huang met Trump at the White House that day along with a number of tech executives. Trump, who had argued previously that the US does not need new AI-specific regulations, said the pact was "morally binding," prompting criticism that it did not lay out consequences for non-compliance.

In the previous week, Huang attended a high-profile state dinner for Xi Jinping at the White House when the Chinese president met Trump.

In mid-September, the Nvidia CEO addressed AI safety concerns during a summit in Los Angeles. He took a phone call from Trump during the event and put him on speaker for the audience. During the roughly five-minute call, Trump called AI safety fears a "hoax."

OCTOBER 2026:

In early October, Trump awarded the National Medal of Science, the United States' highest honor for scientists and engineers, to the Nvidia CEO and some other tech industry leaders.

The same day Trump gave the Nvidia CEO the award, the president disclosed buying up to $1.6 million and selling up to $1 million in Nvidia stock during the summer of 2026.

The Washington Post reported in mid-October that Nvidia committed $25 million for Trump's planned White House ballroom.

NOVEMBER 2026:

Trump said he spoke to the Nvidia boss after the affair between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang - an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, whom US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset - became public.

Trump said on November 9 the Nvidia CEO told him he had no idea that the woman was a spy and that Trump believed the CEO.

"I asked him that question 'Did you have any idea that she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea that she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told a White House briefing.

"I know the FBI is looking into it," Trump said. "I think that he'll be in good shape."

Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; editing by Chris Sanders and Lincoln Feast.

items.title: Guard appears to rebuke Hegseth's delegation at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A US Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier appeared to rebuke Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's delegation on Wednesday after laughter could be heard as they climbed the steps of the solemn site, according to a video of the incident.

Hegseth, his wife and senior aides could be seen taking pictures and speaking to each other on the steps of the memorial at Arlington National Cemetery following a Veterans Day event.

Immediately after the laughter, the sentinel moved toward the group and, from a distance, shouted toward them: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

Sitting at the heart of Arlington National Cemetery, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is a sacred site and the grave of three unknown American service members, including one from World War One. It is widely known as a place for mourning and for reflection on military service, and sentinels guard the site 24 hours a day.

Asked about the incident, which was first reported by CNN, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement: "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored —and will always honor — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."

"While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum," Parnell said.

Hegseth, a former Army National Guard soldier who served in Iraq, prevailed this week after the House of Representatives rejected a Republican lawmaker's effort to impeach him.

At a rare Pentagon press conference on Tuesday hours before the vote, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a farce and defended his record, which includes championing the unpopular Iran war, launching strikes on suspected drug vessels in Latin American waters and firing senior military officers.

Democrats who won control of both chambers of Congress last week have promised to investigate Hegseth for his stewardship of the US military and have not ruled out another impeachment effort.

Reporting by Phil Stewart; Editing by Don Durfee and Edmund Klamann

items.title: Democrat Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat, becomes state's first Black senator since 1874
items.content_html:
Nov 11 (Reuters) - Democratic challenger Scott Colom defeated incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi election for the US Senate, media projected on Wednesday, making him the Southern state's first Black senator since the Reconstruction era that followed the US Civil War.

The result was a stunning upset in the heavily Republican state and expanded on the national drubbing the Democrats delivered to President Donald Trump's Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections. It was also a historic victory for African Americans in a former slave state that was a hotbed of repression during the civil rights movement of the 1960s.

The Mississippi victory gives the Democrats a 55-44 advantage in the 100-member Senate, with the winner in one Senate race from last week's election — in Alaska — yet to be determined. The Democrats have also gained 41 seats in the House of Representatives so far, holding an advantage of 254 to 168 with 13 races yet to be called.

Republicans lost control of both chambers, leaving Trump facing a Democratic-controlled Congress for the first time in either of his two terms and presenting the opposition party with a chance to block highly partisan legislation and investigate Trump's administration.

The Mississippi Senate race was one of the final races to be called after the elections.

The latest media-tabulated results showed Colom ahead by 0.5 percentage point, or some 4,600 votes.

Addressing a gathering of supporters who celebrated his victory with "Senator-Elect Colom" signs, Colom said there were times his long-shot campaign felt defeated but "I had to have faith."

"There were times that I couldn't get donors to answer the phone," Colom said. "They did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith."

"There were times when I was tired, and I felt like I couldn't keep going, but I kept the faith, and that is another tradition of our state," he said.

Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, became the first Democrat to win a Mississippi Senate seat since John Stennis in 1982.

He harnessed frustration over the cost of living with a breakout campaign ad in which voters ridiculed Hyde-Smith's suggestion that consumers had multiple proteins to choose from instead of paying rising prices for beef. Colom's ad rephrased Hyde-Smith's comment with voters saying, "Pick another protein? I'd rather pick another senator instead."

Colom told Reuters in an October interview that Mississippi voters felt betrayed by Trump policies such as the war in Iran, which has driven up fuel prices.

His campaign received a boost from October rallies with two other Black Democratic senators, Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Cory Booker of New Jersey.

HYDE-SMITH CONCEDES

Hyde-Smith, 67, who was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and won a special election later that year, had consistently led opinion polls in a state that Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Trump campaigned in Mississippi for Hyde-Smith near the end of the race.

She congratulated Colom and wished him well in a video posted on social media.

The Democratic victory in Mississippi was a part of a national trend of Democrats finding success in states long dominated by Republicans, including Texas.

With a majority of white voters, Mississippi, deep in the once-segregated South, turned solidly Republican with the political realignment that followed the civil rights movement of the 1960s. Many of the movement's defining battles took place in Mississippi, where Black people faced discrimination in voting, employment, education and public accommodations.

The last Black candidate elected to the Senate in Mississippi was former slave Blanche Bruce in 1874.

attachments.title: Senator-elect Scott Colom smiles during his victory rally at Tougaloo College in Tougaloo, Mississippi, US, on November 11, 2026.

items.title: Migrants trek north through Mexico, buoyed by US election result
items.content_html:
TAPACHULA, Mexico, Nov 11 (Reuters) - More than a thousand migrants were walking northward on Wednesday in a caravan through southern Mexico, spurred by last week's Democratic victory in US midterm elections, which raised hopes that US immigration policies could become more welcoming.

The group, estimated by a Chiapas state government source to number about 1,500 people including many families, set off on Tuesday from the city of Tapachula near the Guatemala border. With possessions in backpacks, parents carried small children in their arms, in strollers or on their shoulders.

Tapachula has long been a key transit point for migrants from Central America heading to the United States.

Due to US entry restrictions and deportations, thousands have become stranded there, where they report a scarcity of jobs, healthcare and schools. Such caravans are common, but many migrants saw new reason for optimism after last week's US elections.

Democrats won control of the US Congress as voters delivered a sharp rebuke to President Donald Trump and his agenda, which includes immigration policies that have increased raids and arrests across parts of the country.

The migrants, mostly from Central America, hope the political shift could open pathways for them to live and work in the United States.

"There might be a light at the end of the tunnel, a way for us to get in," said caravan participant Cesar Sandoval, a 47-year-old Nicaraguan citizen who was deported from the United States a few months ago.

"We believe the Democrats will help us... with God's help," he added before the group, dubbed "God With Us," departed.

The migrants initially aim to reach Mexico City, more than 1,000 km (621 miles) away, to seek assistance from the Mexican federal government and protection from being detained while traveling toward the US border.

The journey to the capital is likely to take at least several weeks, and the migrants carried water in the hot temperatures typical of southern Mexico.

Migrants said the group includes many victims of kidnapping or other crimes in Mexico, and they seek a chance to obtain asylum in the United States.

"For 16 years, I have carried this nightmare in my head. I only ask that the President (Claudia Sheinbaum) be moved and allow us to move forward," said Billy Noe Martinez, a Honduran migrant who survived the 2010 massacre of 72 migrants in Tamaulipas.

"I cannot return to my country because people there are looking for me to kill me, and the same is true in Mexico," he said, recalling that he witnessed fellow migrants being mutilated while still alive and women raped.

Despite the migrants' hopes to enter the US, analysts said potential US policy changes are unlikely to be swift.

"As long as Trump remains president, the deportations will not stop," said Ivan Porraz, a researcher at the College of the Southern Border (Ecosur), who warned that human smugglers could exploit migrants.

Reporting by Damian Sanchez in Tapachula and Lizbeth Diaz in Mexico City; writing by Paolo Laudani; editing by Natalia Siniawski and Cynthia Osterman

attachments.title: A migrant carries a Mexican flag as they journey toward northern Mexico with the goal of reaching the United States, November 10. REUTERS/Damian Sanchez

items.title: Vehicle plows into pedestrians in Los Angeles, killing three
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Nov 10 (Reuters) - An SUV plowed into a group of pedestrians in the North Hollywood district of Los Angeles on Tuesday, killing at least three and critically injuring three more, authorities said.

No official details were immediately available about the incident, which happened shortly before 6 p.m. PST (0200 GMT). A police spokesperson said investigators had yet to determine if the crash was accidental or deliberate.

"We need to understand exactly what happened and what led to this tragedy," Los Angeles County Supervisor Kathryn Barger said in a statement. "I will be closely following the investigation and seeking additional information as the facts emerge."

Three people hit by the vehicle were declared dead at the scene, while two pedestrians and the driver of the vehicle, were taken to hospitals, the Los Angeles police and fire departments said.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said the SUV drove onto a sidewalk and struck a group of street vendors and pedestrians, adding that first responders were on the scene and that her office was working closely with city departments.

"I'm heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted," she added on X, promising updates as more information came in.

Television station KCAL-TV, a CBS News affiliate, said a car crashed into a food stand near a bus stop along Lankershim Boulevard a major road through the busy NoHo commercial and arts district in the city's San Fernando Valley.

A small white partially crumpled SUV appeared to have run up on to the sidewalk under a blue canopy to hit the side of a mass-transit shelter structure, aerial news images from KCAL showed.

Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles and Jasper Ward and Kanishka Singh in Washington and Rhea Rose Abraham in Bengaluru; Editing by Michelle Nichols, Lincoln Feast and Clarence Fernandez

items.title: Baby boy found alive in US after believed buried for 24 hours, police say
items.content_html:
Nov 10 (Reuters) - An 11-month-old boy was found alive in South Carolina on Tuesday after he was believed to have been buried for about 24 hours, the Lexington County Sheriff's Department said.

The infant, Koah Sharpe, was found wrapped in a towel in a dog crate, shallowly buried in woods, according to the department.

"Certainly God is good. Just a few moments ago, we found little Koah, 11 months old, buried alive, clinging to life, crying — the most joyful sound you ever heard of a crying baby," Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said during a news conference.

Koon said the infant's father, Michael Comer, was arrested on Monday night on burglary and resisting arrest. The department is working with the solicitor's office to determine additional charges, he said.

Koah went missing on Monday after being left in his father's care at his mother's home while she ran an errand, Koon said. The boy was reported missing and authorities began a widespread search, according to the sheriff.

Koah was found after a search party discovered "freshly disturbed" dirt in the woods about 50 yards from Comer's father's house, Koon said.

The infant is currently at the hospital and will "hopefully" recover, the sheriff said.

Reporting by Jasper Ward in Washington; editing by Michelle Nichols

items.title: Kennedy family tries to stop Trump's Washington arch
items.content_html:
Nov 10 (Reuters) - Several members of the Kennedy family, one of America's most famous political dynasties, filed on Tuesday to join a court case aimed at stopping President Donald Trump from building a proposed triumphal arch in Washington, saying it would obstruct views and cast shadows over their relatives' grave sites.

The 250-foot (76-meter) arch, shown in a rendering to include a flame held by a 60-foot gold winged female figure and flanked by gold flying eagles, would be situated across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial on a highway roundabout near the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery.

A judge has already issued a temporary order blocking construction through November 19 as she considers whether to issue a preliminary injunction.

The arch "will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sight lines to the existing grave sites and memorials established in the Kennedy family's honor at Arlington National Cemetery, as well as to the memorials of hundreds of thousands of fallen American heroes," the filing said.

The Kennedy family is one of the most prolific political dynasties in US history, notably including former President John F. Kennedy. Trump's health secretary is Robert F. Kennedy Jr., nephew of the assassinated former president.

"It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery," a White House spokesman said in a statement, adding that the Trump administration would continue to make the case for the monument.

The Trump administration contends Congress approved the arch more than 100 years ago when it also authorized construction of a bridge across the Potomac River. It has said that the arch would honor veterans.

Numerous Democrats in Congress have vowed to block construction once they take control in January, after winning November's midterm elections.

Additional reporting by David Shepardson; editing by Michelle Nichols

items.title: US House Republicans elect Jim Jordan as leader for next Congress, Punchbowl News reports
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Republicans in the US House of Representatives elected conservative Jim Jordan on Tuesday to lead their conference as minority leader during the final two years of President Donald Trump's presidency, Punchbowl News reported.

A secret ballot party held behind closed doors elevated the Ohio Republican and House Judiciary Committee chairman to the minority leadership post a week after Democrats swept to victory last Tuesday's midterm elections, winning sizable majorities in both the House and Senate.

items.title: US House votes to derail impeachment of Defense Secretary Hegseth
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Republicans in the US House of Representatives banded together on Tuesday to derail an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The chamber voted 211 to 204 in favor of a motion to refer the impeachment charges to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, effectively stopping the effort to impeach Hegseth sponsored by Kentucky Republican Representative Thomas Massie.

Massie was the only Republican who voted against the motion.

Reporting by Patricia Zengerle; Editing by Chris Reese

REUTERS/Annabelle Gordon

items.title: House Democrats to investigate Trump's handling of US spy agencies
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Democrats in the US House of Representatives, who will control key committees next year, are preparing investigations into what they say was President Donald Trump's politicization and gutting of US spy agencies, including whether analysts have censored themselves to avoid retaliation.

"There's absolutely evidence that analysts are hesitant to write on topics that they think might be controversial. There's absolutely evidence of a decline in morale in the analytic community because of the pressures that they are under," US Representative Jim Himes, a Connecticut Democrat who will become chairman of the House intelligence committee in January, told Reuters on Tuesday.

There has been little scrutiny of the state of the US intelligence community by the Republican-run Congress during the first two years of Trump's second term, during which the administration fired or forced out hundreds of officers and disrupted the production of analyses on key issues, including Iran.

Himes said that would change after he takes over the committee in January, when Democrats assume control of the House of Representatives and the Senate following their sweep of the November 3 midterm elections.

He did not disclose how the investigations would proceed, but said that one focus would be what he called retaliatory firings.

"We're going to tell the story of the patriots who were fired because they said something that was inconsistent with what the president wanted to be true," Himes said.

Former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard last year cut her agency's staff by about 40%. CIA Director John Ratcliffe publicly pledged to reduce his workforce by more than 1,000 positions over several years. Both offered deferred-resignation programs that provided pay and benefits for employees who chose to leave.

The cuts included the firings of longtime intelligence analysts and officers from top posts, including at the National Intelligence Council, the analytical group overseen by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

At least two of those fired were analysts involved in an assessment that contradicted the White House's official policy on Venezuela.

The reductions have been viewed inside the intelligence agencies as a continuation of Trump's campaign against what he called the "deep state," a move critics say has drained the community of experience and expertise.

Reuters previously reported that some of Gabbard's projects affiliated with her Director's Initiative Group, a task force that revisited the 2020 election and the origins of COVID-19, created tensions inside the intelligence community.

BREAKDOWN IN INTELLIGENCE SHARING

That was particularly the case after Gabbard's office revoked the security clearances of current and former intelligence officials a year ago.

Gabbard's actions caused a breakdown in intelligence sharing and cooperation inside the intelligence community and with Congress, as Reuters previously reported.

"The moment the intelligence community stops telling the truth to national leaders, you get into an Iraq war because of weapons of mass destruction that don't exist," Himes said.

Himes said he had reviewed a statutorily mandated intelligence community survey showing that, in 2025, the workforce had begun to "feel very real political pressure."

He added he was working to declassify other internal intelligence community reporting that could potentially underscore the effects of the firings and politicization.

The committee, Himes said, will also probe the administration's relationships with defense and intelligence contractors and US covert efforts overseas.

Reporting by Erin Banco and Jonathan Landay; Editing by Don Durfee and Sanjeev Miglani

items.title: US consumer prices rise briskly for third straight month
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - US consumer prices increased more than expected in October amid higher costs for food and accommodation, cementing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month.

The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Tuesday also showed a strong buildup of underlying inflation pressures for a third straight month. It followed data last week showing the labor market regained momentum in October.

Inflation is being driven by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has boosted oil prices, the Trump administration's import tariffs, resilient consumer spending and aggressive business investment in artificial intelligence technology.

The rising cost of living contributed to the heavy losses suffered by President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the midterm elections last week.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday the US central bank should raise rates next month, adding that "a stronger policy move may be needed." Waller also raised the prospect of an aggressive 50-basis-point hike.

"The Fed seems to be falling behind the curve on inflation, and the October hold is looking like a policy mistake," said Stephen Juneau, an economist at Bank of America Securities. "We see a rising risk that the Fed will have to hike again in January, rather than March."

The CPI increased 0.4% last month after advancing 0.6% in September, the department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said. It was the third consecutive month of gains of 0.4% or more. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI would climb 0.3% over the month. The BLS did not publish year-over-year inflation readings because last year's federal government shutdown prevented the collection of consumer price data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base.

Some economists used the average index for September and November 2025 to estimate the year-over-year rate of change for the October CPI. Others used interpolated levels from independent sources. Their estimates for the October year-over-year CPI ranged from a gain of 3.9% to 4.0%. Annual consumer inflation was 3.7% in September.

Shelter, which includes rents and hotel and motel rooms, accounted for more than 30% of the monthly increase in the CPI. Shelter costs rose 0.3% after climbing 0.4% in September.

Food prices surged 0.5% after barely rising in the prior three months. Grocery store prices climbed 0.4%, boosted by a 0.9% jump in the cost of beef. Egg prices rose 0.6%, while fruits and vegetables were 0.6% more expensive. Prices for dairy products increased 0.6%. The cost of snacks surged 1.0%.

Rising prices at the supermarket could be an early sign that high diesel prices are filtering through to consumers. The cost of eating out also increased last month, with prices of food away from home rising 0.5% after a 0.2% gain in September. The cost of full-service meals jumped 0.7%.

"This may finally be the beginning of a pass-through of higher transportation costs to grocery prices," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets. "If this is indeed happening, it could be a feature across a broad array of goods categories."

Gasoline prices climbed 1.0% after soaring 9.1% in September. Consumers also paid more for electricity. Although diesel prices have eased off all-time highs, they remain on an upward trend, rising 2.7% in October after increasing 11.9% in September.

Consumers could get some relief at the pump, with oil prices down at least 10% so far this month, but the pressure is unlikely to ease elsewhere, economists warned.

Inflation-adjusted average weekly earnings fell again in October.

MORE RATE HIKES ANTICIPATED

The so-called core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy items, increased 0.3% in October for the third straight month. The so-called core CPI was forecast to have climbed 0.2% in October. Economists estimated that year-over-year core CPI inflation gained 2.8% in October. Annual core CPI inflation rose 2.6% in September.

Financial markets are pricing in a roughly 89% chance of a 25-basis-point rate hike next month, and expect another increase in March, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed. The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month. Economists said only a substantial selloff in equity markets or widening credit spreads would prevent the Fed from tightening monetary policy in December.

Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower. They slumped last week after the Democrats' sweeping victory fanned fears that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade, but rallied on Monday as oil prices fell. The dollar gained against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields were mostly higher.

Underlying inflation last month was driven by a 0.3% rise in owners' equivalent rent, a measure of the amount homeowners would pay to rent or earn from renting their property. Prices for hotel and motel rooms rose 0.6%. Airline fares increased 0.4%. The cost of recreation services climbed 0.9%, while that of motor vehicle insurance advanced 0.7%.

Doctor visits and hospital services also cost more. But the price of health insurance dropped 1.8%. The BLS updated the data used to calculate this component. Overall services prices excluding energy increased 0.3% after rising 0.4% in September.

Tariff effects were also evident in October. Prices of household furnishings and supplies rebounded 0.7% and the cost of toys increased 1.8%. There were more price gains for computers and peripherals, reflecting the AI spending boom. Prices for smartphones rose a record 1.4%.

There were also increases in the prices of new vehicles and medication. But used car and truck prices dropped 1.2%. Core goods prices increased 0.2% after climbing 0.3% in September.

The missing data from last year have no impact on the calculation of the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index readings that the Fed tracks to gauge progress toward its inflation target.

Based on last month's data, economists estimated that core PCE inflation rose 0.4% after advancing 0.3% in September. In the 12 months through October, core PCE inflation is projected to have increased 3.3% after gaining 3.1% in the 12 months through September. These estimates could be impacted by producer price data for October that is due to be released on Friday.

"Inflation isn't dead; it is very much alive and the cost-of-living crisis rages on," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS.

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Paul Simao

items.title: US traffic deaths fall in first half of 2026, lowest rate since 2014
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - US traffic deaths fell in the first half of this year to the lowest rate since 2014, the government said on Tuesday, retreating from a spike during the 2020 COVID pandemic and several years in which road deaths remained elevated.

This year is on pace to be the fifth straight year of declines, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which said traffic deaths dropped 2.5% to 16,750 in the first half of the year. It was the lowest number since 2015 and down from 17,175 in the same period last year.

The fatality rate fell to 1.02 fatalities per 100 million vehicle miles traveled and the number of deaths fell to the lowest number since 2015.

Full-year traffic deaths for 2025 fell to the lowest number since 2019 and the fatality rate fell to 1.10 fatalities per 100 million vehicle miles traveled, the second-lowest yearly figure in US history, NHTSA said.

Deaths fell 5% in the first three months of 2026 but just 0.2% in the second three months.

One area of concern remains bicyclist deaths, which rose 4% to 1,148 last year. In 2023, bicyclist deaths hit their highest figure in more than four decades.

US traffic deaths jumped 10.8% in 2021 to 43,230, the most in a single year since 2005.

As US roads became less crowded during the pandemic, some motorists perceived police as less likely to issue tickets, experts said, resulting in riskier driving. Some drivers were also more likely to drive while being impaired by alcohol or drugs consumed at home during the pandemic.

The US fatality rate rose much higher than for other developed nations during the pandemic.

A 2023 NHTSA study found crashes directly cost taxpayers $30 billion, and society as a whole $340 billion. When quality-of-life valuations were included, the total cost to society ran to $1.37 trillion.

items.title: Most Americans want new Democratic Congress to end Trump's Iran war, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Majorities of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress to act to end the war with Iran and to repeal tariffs put in place by President Donald Trump, signaling demand for quick action to address the high cost of living, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

The four-day poll, completed on Monday, showed 71% of Americans -- including 93% of Democrats and 51% of Republicans -- want US Congress to pass legislation ending the conflict with Iran that Trump launched alongside US ally Israel in February.

Democrats won their largest majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives since at least 2008 in last week's midterm elections, in a sharp rebuke to Trump's Republicans over high costs and a deeply unpopular war. Democrats will take power when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.

A smaller but still-significant share of respondents -- 62% -- said they would support an effort to repeal tariffs on imports put in place by the Trump administration.

The war with Iran has pushed fuel prices sharply higher, adding to inflation already stoked by the new taxes Trump slapped on hundreds of imported goods. Trump has defended the war as necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. The tariffs, he has said, will boost American industry by protecting it from cheap imports.

Democratic Party leaders have vowed to address cost of living concerns, and say they will try to force an end to the US war with Iran. Many in the party have also vowed to end Trump's tariffs.

DESIRE FOR BIPARTISANSHIP

Large majorities of people in both political parties said it was important for Trump to make an effort to work with Democrats and for Democratic leaders in the new Congress to try to work with the president.

Nine in 10 respondents said cost of living issues should be a focus for the Congress during its first 100 days. Smaller shares wanted a focus on issues like artificial intelligence regulation, immigration reform and climate change.

OPPOSITION TO IMPEACHMENT

But many Americans appear concerned Democrats will use their new power to launch legal proceedings against Trump. Some 42% of poll respondents said it would be "bad for the country" if the new Congress tried to impeach Trump, compared with 33% who said it would be good for the country. The rest weren't sure or didn't answer the question.

Congressional Democrats are divided on how to bring down healthcare costs, and also disagree on how aggressively to target Trump, including whether to impeach the president or members of his cabinet. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is expected to face a House impeachment vote this week, following a move by a Republican lawmaker.

While Trump said after the elections he would "probably" get along with Democrats, he also promoted Stephen Miller, a polarizing aide who has called the Democratic Party a domestic extremist group, to be his new White House chief of staff.

While the poll showed Trump's approval rating near the lowest level of his political career, at 32%, it also showed Democrats were not particularly popular either.

Some 45% of Americans had a favorable view of Democrats, while 51% had an unfavorable view. Some 35% had a favorable view of Republicans and 60% viewed them unfavorably.

Asked which party had a better approach to regulating artificial intelligence, which could be an important issue for Congress in the coming months, 28% picked Democrats and 20% picked Republicans while the rest said they weren't sure or that neither was better.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, gathered responses from 1,705 US adults and had a margin of error of about 2 percentage points.

Reporting by Jason Lange in Washington; editing by Scott Malone and Deepa Babington

items.title: India, US continuing talks to finalise first tranche of trade deal, official says
items.content_html:
Nov 10 (Reuters) - India is continuing talks with the US to finalise the first tranche of a bilateral trade deal, and US officials visited the country earlier this month for discussions, an Indian official told reporters on Tuesday.

Discussions earlier this month centred on customs and trade facilitation issues, the official added.

The comments come after US President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the November 3 midterm elections, losing control of both chambers of the US Congress.

With some races still undecided, Democrats scored their biggest victory in the House of Representatives since at least 2008 while flipping Senate seats in traditionally conservative states including Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

Reporting by Shivangi Acharya in New Delhi. Writing by Kanjyik Ghosh in Barcelona. Editing by Mark Potter
